title: Is This the World’s Oldest Image of a Mind‑altering Plant?
gist: An anthropologist argues that five red bell-shaped signs painted 17,000-15,000 years ago in Spain's El Castillo cave depict a psychoactive nightshade like belladonna or henbane, which if confirmed would be the oldest known image of a mind-altering plant by thousands of years.

themes.theme: The El Castillo panel and its reinterpretation

insights.claim: A small painted panel in a side passage of El Castillo cave in northern Spain shows five red bell-shaped signs created roughly 17,000 to 15,000 years ago, sitting above a natural stone ledge resembling an altar.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Establishes the physical setting and age of the artwork at the center of the reinterpretation.
insights.quote: Created some 17,000 to 15,000 years ago, it shows five red signs, each shaped a little like a bell.

insights.claim: For over a century archaeologists have simply catalogued the El Castillo bell-shaped signs as unexplained ice age marks without assigning them meaning.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Shows how long the panel sat unexamined for a plant-based reading before this reinterpretation.
insights.quote: For over a century, archaeologists have simply catalogued these as “bell-shaped signs,” filed under the vast heading of ice age marks we don’t know the meaning of.

insights.claim: Building on his PhD research surveying plants used in shamanic ritual worldwide, Benjamin Pothier argues the El Castillo signs may depict mind-altering flowers, most likely belladonna or a local henbane.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Central thesis of the piece: reframes an unexplained Palaeolithic motif as evidence of early plant-based ritual knowledge.
insights.quote: Building on my Ph.D. research surveying plants used in shamanic ritual worldwide, I argue they may be flowers.

insights.claim: Pothier previously published a 2021 paper making a similar plant-identification argument about a tree drawn on the Chu Silk Manuscript, China's oldest illustrated text.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Shows the author has a track record applying this plant-in-art identification method to another ancient culture.
insights.quote: I published a paper in 2021 making a similar case for a tree drawn on the Chu Silk Manuscript, China’s oldest illustrated text.

insights.claim: If Pothier's interpretation is correct, the El Castillo signs would be the oldest known picture of a mind-altering plant anywhere in the world, by thousands of years.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: States the headline-level stakes of the claim explicitly.
insights.quote: If my interpretation is correct, then these unremarkable red signs would be the oldest known picture of a mind-altering plant anywhere in the world, by thousands of years.

insights.claim: At Pinwheel Cave in California, chewed bits of hallucinogenic plant matter wedged into the rock gave the first unambiguous physical proof anywhere in the world that a plant depicted in rock art had actually been ingested at the site.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Offers a precedent method by which the El Castillo hypothesis could someday be physically corroborated.
insights.quote: It could be corroborated the way it was at Pinwheel Cave in California, where chewed bits of hallucinogenic plant matter found wedged into the rock gave the first unambiguous physical proof anywhere in the world that a plant depicted in rock art had been ingested at the site.

themes.theme: Visual case for a nightshade flower

insights.claim: The El Castillo signs share a drooping, five-lobed, flared bell silhouette with a central vein-like line, closely matching the shape of a belladonna flower.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Core visual evidence underpinning the botanical identification.
insights.quote: The El Castillo signs share this silhouette—the flared bell, the downward hang, and, on several, a central line echoing the vein of the living flower.

insights.claim: Henbane, another psychoactive nightshade native to the region, produces a similarly bell-shaped flower at certain stages of growth, offering a second plausible botanical match for the signs.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Broadens the candidate plant identifications beyond a single species, strengthening the general nightshade-flower reading.
insights.quote: Henbane, another psychoactive nightshade native to the region, produces a similarly shaped bell at certain stages of its growth.

insights.claim: Pothier argues the deliberate grouping of the signs, the altar-like stone ledge beneath them, and independent evidence that prehistoric Europeans knew these plants intimately together lift the resemblance above mere coincidence.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Explains the author's reasoning for treating a visual resemblance as meaningful rather than accidental.
insights.quote: What I feel lifts these signs above coincidence is the company they keep: the deliberate grouping, the altar-like ledge, and the weight of independent evidence that prehistoric Europeans knew these plants intimately.
insights.locator: Some might argue that a bell is a simple form

insights.claim: French archaeologist André Leroi-Gourhan's mid-20th-century framework catalogued ovals, triangles, and rounded forms across Palaeolithic sites, including bell-shaped signs, as vulvar or female symbols.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Identifies the dominant prior interpretive paradigm that the new botanical reading has to contend with.
insights.quote: Following the French archaeologist André Leroi-Gourhan’s mid 20th-century framework, ovals, triangles, and rounded forms across Palaeolithic sites like these bell-shaped signs were often catalogued as vulvar or female symbols.

insights.claim: Paleoanthropologist Genevieve von Petzinger and other specialists have pushed back on the vulvar-symbol interpretive lens, arguing it reflects the assumptions of largely male early researchers as much as the evidence itself.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Signals that the field's older symbolic frameworks are already contested on methodological grounds, opening space for alternative readings like the plant hypothesis.
insights.quote: Some specialists, including Canadian paleoanthropologist Genevieve von Petzinger, have since pushed back on this once-dominant interpretive lens.

themes.theme: Nightshades in later European ritual history

insights.claim: The active compounds in nightshades—atropine, scopolamine, and hyoscyamine—produce vivid hallucinations and a striking sensation that one's skin is sprouting fur or feathers.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Grounds the shamanic-transformation reading of related Palaeolithic art in specific, documented pharmacological effects.
insights.quote: Their active compounds—atropine, scopolamine, hyoscyamine—produce vivid hallucinations and the striking sensation that one’s skin is sprouting fur or feathers.

insights.claim: The fur/feather hallucination associated with nightshade compounds echoes ice-age part-human, part-animal figures such as the 40,000-year-old lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel and the antlered 'sorcerer' figures in French caves, long read as shamans mid-transformation.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Suggests a possible pharmacological explanation for a much wider category of Palaeolithic hybrid-figure imagery, not just the El Castillo panel.
insights.quote: This has echoes of the part-human, part-animal figures common in ice age art, from the lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel—a 40,000-year-old ivory carving with a human body and the head of a cave lion—and the “sorcerers” of French caves.
insights.locator: This has echoes of the part-human, part-animal figures

insights.claim: Chemical analysis of Bronze Age human hair from the Es Càrritx burial cave in Menorca confirms people consumed multiple psychoactive compounds, including atropine and scopolamine, around 3,000 years ago.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Provides direct chemical (not just iconographic) evidence that nightshade psychoactives were consumed in prehistoric Europe.
insights.quote: Chemical analysis of Bronze Age human hair from the burial cave of Es Càrritx in Menorca confirms people there consumed multiple psychoactive compounds, atropine and scopolamine among them, around 3,000 years ago.

insights.claim: Belladonna's ritual use threads through European history up to the 15th-to-17th-century witch trials in Germany, France, and Italy, where it was a staple ingredient of the 'flying ointments' said to carry witches to the sabbath.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Shows a continuous documented thread of belladonna ritual use that the author is trying to trace back to the Palaeolithic.
insights.quote: Belladonna’s use threads through European history right up to the witch trials in Germany, France and Italy, roughly from the 15th to 17th centuries, where it was considered a staple of the “flying ointments” said to carry witches to the sabbath.
insights.locator: Belladonna’s use threads through European history

themes.theme: Chronology, scarcity of evidence, and testability

insights.claim: The oldest previously widely discussed candidate images of mind-altering plants, the 'mushroom' figures of Tassili n'Ajjer in the Algerian Sahara, date to roughly 7,000 to 9,000 years ago.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Sets the benchmark record the El Castillo panel would beat if the identification holds.
insights.quote: The famous “mushroom” figures of Tassili n'Ajjer in the Sahara… have been read by some researchers as an early depiction of ritual mushroom use. The oldest widely discussed candidates date to roughly 7,000 to 9,000 years ago.

insights.claim: According to a chronological study of the cave's iconographic layering, the El Castillo panel belongs to the lower Magdalenian period, some 17,000 to 15,000 years ago, which would push the earliest known plant image back 7,000 to 10,000 years into the upper Palaeolithic.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Quantifies exactly how large a chronological leap the claim represents versus prior evidence.
insights.quote: That would push the picture back 7,000 to 10,000 years, into the upper Palaeolithic.

insights.claim: A 2023 survey of 5,786 catalogued images across 113 European Palaeolithic caves found plants account for just 0.07 percent of them, versus over half for animals, meaning plant depictions are exceedingly rare and possibly under-recognized.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete reason for caution: the claim rests on almost no comparable examples, though this scarcity itself may be a research-bias artifact.
insights.quote: A 2023 survey of 5,786 catalogued images across 113 European Palaeolithic caves found that plants account for just 0.07 percent of them, against over half for animals.

insights.claim: At Chauvet Cave in southeastern France, a cave bear skull was deliberately placed on a flat stone block with traces of a fire lit beneath it, forming an altar-like arrangement roughly 36,000 years old.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Provides a precedent for deliberate shrine-like arrangements in Palaeolithic caves, supporting the plausibility of an altar reading at El Castillo.
insights.quote: At Chauvet Cave in southeastern France, a cave bear skull was deliberately placed on a flat stone block, with traces of a fire lit beneath it, in what excavators have described as an altar-like arrangement roughly 36,000 years old.

insights.claim: Modern techniques for recovering ancient environmental DNA from sediment are sensitive enough that traces of Solanaceae (the nightshade family) could be detected beneath the El Castillo panel, offering a concrete future test of the hypothesis.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: Names a specific, falsifiable scientific method that could confirm or refute the plant-identification claim.
insights.quote: Modern techniques for recovering ancient environmental DNA from sediment are sensitive enough that traces of Solanaceae—the nightshade family, which includes belladonna and henbane—could support the reading.

insights.claim: Pothier frames the claim as deliberately testable: a future field study could either confirm it via sediment DNA or disprove it, and either outcome would be scientifically valuable.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Pothier
insights.so_what: If confirmed, the claim would mean image-making and mind-altering plant use are entangled at the very origin of human art.
insights.quote: If wrong, a field study will show it. If right, it would mean the human impulse to make images and the human use of mind-altering plants are entangled at the very origin of art.
